activities.anchor: The discipline has a characteristic rhythm
activities.caption: rebuild the EDA rhythm
activities.name: edaRhythmOrder

config.prompt: Rebuild the exploratory rhythm in order:
items: Plot everything — distributions, relationships, segments, time
Question what you see — is it real, a bug, a segment?
Re-plot to test the question — and write down what surprised you
config.why: Plot, notice, question, re-plot — the loop that Tukey turned into a method, and whose deliverable is hypotheses, not a model.

activities.anchor: A histogram or density plot per variable
activities.caption: pair each distribution feature with what it decides
activities.name: edaDistMatch

config.prompt: Pair each distribution feature with its consequence:

pairs.right: two populations in one column — a single-number summary averages them into fiction
punish linear models, reward medians and log scales
survive outliers that wreck means and ranges

config.why: Shape, centre, spread, tails — read all four before trusting any summary the distribution feeds.

activities.caption: bet before you read on — read the gap
activities.name: edaSkewPredict

config.q: A retail dataset's orders: median 24, mean 89. What does the histogram most likely look like?
choices: Strongly right-skewed — most orders small, a thin spike of enormous ones
Left-skewed — a few very small orders dragging the mean down
config.why: The mean–median gap measures skew: a mean far above the median is the signature of a long right tail — most orders small, a few enormous ones dragging the average up.

activities.anchor: Correlation matrices give the overview but inherit linear blinders
activities.caption: find the backwards claim — what correlation cannot do
activities.name: edaCorrSpot

config.prompt: One of these claims about correlation is backwards — click it:
lines: Correlation matrices give the overview; scatter plots handle anything important.
Jitter or alpha-blend dense scatters, or thousands of points hide as a solid blob.
A U-shaped relationship scores near zero on linear correlation.
A single outlier cannot move a correlation much either way.
config.correction: A single outlier can manufacture or destroy a strong correlation on its own — remove one point and a strong relationship can vanish; add one and it can appear.
config.why: Correlation is a question, not an answer — it only sees straight lines, and the scatter plot decides about the relationship.

activities.caption: the aggregate is accused — run the check
activities.name: edaSimpsonBranch

config.root: Berkeley 1973: men admitted at 44%, women at 35%. Someone declares bias proven.

start.text: What do you check before concluding?

choices.label: Slice by department and compare the slices to the total
choices.feedback: Department by department, women did as well or better — the reversal came from application patterns.

choices.label: Accept the aggregate — it is the real number
choices.feedback: The aggregate was true and misleading simultaneously — the average of several opposite stories.

choices.label: Collect a bigger sample and recompute the total
choices.feedback: More rows of the same aggregation reproduce the same reversal — the aggregation level is the decision.

paradox.text: Women applied disproportionately to the most competitive departments; men to engineering's high-rate departments.

choices.label: So what is the honest headline?
choices.feedback: 'Admission rates differed by department' — the correct response to 'what is the overall number?' is often 'for whom?'

aggregate.text: A true number that tells the opposite story — Simpson's paradox is the proof that aggregation is a modelling decision.

bigger.text: Sample size fixes noise, not reversals — the paradox survives any n.

whom.text: Slice, compare, and report the structure — that is the finding that matters.

config.why: The aggregate can be the average of several opposite stories — every important relationship gets sliced by its natural segments.

activities.anchor: Any column with a timestamp earns a line plot
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the time-plot reading list
activities.name: edaTimeCloze

config.text: Time plots get their own reading list: %%0%% (the long slope), %%1%% (the repeating daily, weekly or yearly pattern), %%2%% (level changes at specific dates — usually interventions, sometimes bugs), and %%3%% (outliers to investigate, not smooth away).
config.hint: The slope, the rhythm, the step, and the one-day wonder.

activities.anchor: Hunt through twenty slices and something will look significant
activities.caption: file each act under generation or prosecution
activities.name: edaLoopSort

config.prompt: File each act under the activity it belongs to:

items.label: find data-quality bugs in a plot that makes no sense
test the pattern on data the exploration did not use
state the pattern as a hypothesis a test could refute

config.why: Exploration is generation, generous with patterns; confirmation is prosecution, hostile to them — the honest workflow keeps the two notebooks separate.

activities.anchor: tip is zero for 60% of trips
activities.caption: call the no-tip share
activities.name: edaTipEst

config.prompt: In the rideshare trip table, what share of trips had exactly zero tip?
config.why: 60% — a bimodal flag, not an error: one regime tips, one does not, and the split turned out to follow pickup zones.
config.context: a single-number average tip would have buried the segmentation

activities.anchor: Fit a model — even a simple line — and its
activities.caption: residuals with structure versus clean scatter — drag the divider
activities.name: edaResidCompare

config.prompt: Two verdicts a residual plot can deliver — drag the divider:

before.label: structure left in
before.text: curvature a straight line flattened, seasonality the trend ignored, a segment behaving differently — patterns the model missed

after.label: clean scatter
after.text: no structure the eye can find — the model captured what this data offers

config.why: Each model is a hypothesis about structure, and its residuals are the data's answer to it — which is why the EDA → model → EDA loop advances.
